Faisla Finserv: One Ledger, Two Customers

A Bengaluru lending-infrastructure company must decide whether to keep selling credit to businesses, start selling it to consumers, or try to do both without breaking either.

A teaching case for Strategy & Business — Product Strategy

1. The Scene

On the morning of 28 September 2026, Ananya Rao sat in the tenth-floor conference room of Faisla Finserv's office on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road, reading the same board deck for the fourth time. In fourteen days she would present Faisla's FY27 strategy to the board, and a letter of intent from a Singapore growth fund — a possible ₹180 crore Series C — was conditional on answering one question the term sheet spelled out in bold: would Faisla remain a business selling lending infrastructure to other companies, or build a lending product that reached Indian consumers directly? Ananya had founded Faisla in 2019 to do the former. Nothing since had prepared her to decide the latter in two weeks, with a client in Dubai threatening to walk and her own data science lead insisting the opportunity would not wait for certainty.

2. Company Background

Faisla Finserv did not lend money; it lent the machinery of lending. Its core product was an API that let e-commerce platforms and retail point-of-sale systems offer "buy now, pay in 3" checkout financing without building credit underwriting themselves. Faisla scored the borrower using transaction data supplied by its client, priced the loan, and passed the application to a partner non-banking financial company that disbursed the funds — the structure Indian regulation required after the RBI's 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines and 2023 default-loss-guarantee framework drew a firm line between the fintech that originates a loan and the regulated entity that carries it. Faisla operated as what the RBI called a Lending Service Provider, taking a fee on every loan it helped originate rather than interest income itself.

By FY26, fourteen clients used the Faisla API, the two largest being Fanoos Commerce Cloud, a Pune-based reseller marketplace competing with Meesho and Flipkart's seller network in tier-2 towns, and Farasha Retail LLC, a Dubai-headquartered electronics and apparel marketplace that used Faisla for instalment checkout during Diwali and Eid sales. Rivals Setu, Perfios, and Razorpay's own lending stack chased the same clients, keeping Faisla's take rate under constant pressure. Ananya's founding bet was that owning the underwriting layer, not the balance sheet, was where the durable margin sat. Revenue had grown from ₹6 crore in FY22 to ₹42 crore in FY26, profitable at the operating level for the first time that year.

3. The Situation

The pressure had built from two directions at once. Inside the company, Priya Iyer, Faisla's Toronto-based head of data science, had spent eighteen months arguing that the underwriting model built for checkout financing — trained on years of repayment behaviour across Faisla's client base — was accurate enough to lend directly to consumers, and that rivals like KreditBee and Bajaj Finserv were proving the market's appetite. Outside the company, the Series C term sheet had arrived with a note from the fund's Singapore partner that Faisla's total addressable market, sold purely as B2B infrastructure, was "respectable but not venture-scale." Consumer lending, the note argued, was a ten-times larger prize.

Then, on 19 September, Karan Mehta — Faisla's VP of B2B Partnerships, in Gurugram — took a call from Farasha Retail LLC's country manager in Dubai. Word had reached her that Faisla was exploring its own consumer lending app. If true, Farasha would treat Faisla as a future competitor, not a vendor, and would start evaluating Setu as a replacement before its March renewal. Fanoos Commerce Cloud's founder, hearing the same rumour secondhand, asked Karan directly whether Faisla intended to disintermediate its own retail clients. Karan had no clean answer, and said so in the Slack thread that convinced Ananya the board meeting could no longer be postponed.

Two colleagues shaped the decision without sitting at the table: Elena Fischer, Faisla's design lead in Berlin, had quietly sketched a consumer app "in case," and Wei Ling Tan, the Singapore-based customer-success lead on the Farasha account, was the one relaying how nervous Dubai had become.

6. The Options

Option A — Stay B2B, go deeper

Decline the consumer pivot; invest the Series C in embedding further into existing clients (fraud scoring, GST-linked invoice financing for Fanoos's kirana partners). Upside: protects the Farasha and Fanoos relationships and the trust underlying Faisla's whole client base; keeps the balance-sheet-light model intact. Cost: a smaller TAM story that may cost the round if the fund walks away from a "respectable but not venture-scale" business.

Option B — Launch B2C, sunset conflicting accounts

Build the consumer lending app Priya has urged, obtain or partner for an NBFC licence, and accept that clients whose shoppers Faisla would now court directly — starting with Farasha — will leave. Upside: roughly doubles projected revenue and answers the investor's growth question. Cost: real client defection already signalled by Farasha and Fanoos, new regulatory capital and compliance burden, and unproven consumer underwriting at scale.

Option C — Ring-fence a separate consumer brand

Launch the consumer product under a distinct brand and legal entity, walled off from the B2B business, while Faisla's API keeps serving Fanoos and any client willing to stay. Upside: a credible answer to existing clients while still pursuing the consumer opportunity and a larger growth story. Cost: two go-to-market motions, two operating models, and a bet that clients believe a wall exists — Farasha's manager was explicit that shared ownership alone would break trust, whatever the branding.

7. Questions for Discussion

  1. What does Faisla actually sell today — infrastructure or credit — and how does that shape what its clients believe they are owed?
  2. Read Exhibits 1 and 2 together. Which should carry more weight: the FY27 revenue upside, or the unit economics and capital behind it?
  3. Is the Farasha/Fanoos conflict a true either/or, or can Option C's separation credibly resolve it? What would make Farasha believe the wall is real?
  4. What would you tell the board about the difference between growing a B2B strategy and switching to a B2C one — and what should Ananya decide by 12 October?

8. A Note for the Learner

The B2B-versus-B2C lens exists because the two are not points on one spectrum but different businesses: different customers, sales motions, and economics, and — as this case shows — sometimes customers of each other. A well-reasoned answer does three things. First, it treats the client-trust problem as seriously as the revenue opportunity: Farasha and Fanoos are Faisla's actual FY26 revenue, and channel conflict with a B2B base is a strategic cost, not a branding problem. Second, it reads Exhibit 2, not just Exhibit 1, as the real argument — a business with 2.1% NPAs, no capital requirement, and existing profitability should not be abandoned for one with 5.4% NPAs and an 18–24 month breakeven merely because the addressable market looks larger on a slide. Third, it recognises Faisla's edge — underwriting built from B2B transaction data — as a capability, not a mandate to enter every market that capability could theoretically serve.

On that reasoning, Option A is the defensible path, with one amendment: Ananya should tell the board that Faisla will not chase a consumer TAM it cannot serve without breaking the trust its client base is built on, and should redirect the Series C toward deepening the B2B product — invoice financing for Fanoos's kirana network is the more credible growth line, since it grows revenue per existing client rather than manufacturing a new, uncertain one. Option C should be named and explicitly rejected in the deck, not ignored, because investors will ask: Karan's evidence from Farasha already shows clients will not believe the wall, whatever the entity structure. If the Singapore partner still finds the story too small, that is a signal about whether this investor fits a company whose advantage is depth in one market, not breadth across two.

B2B vs B2C Strategy: What Survives Contact With the Buying Committee

An advanced treatment for practitioners who already know that the buyer and the user can be different people. This page is about what follows from that fact once you take it seriously: the arithmetic of approval chains, the structural scarcity of expansion revenue in consumer businesses, the low-sample-size problem that makes B2B product management a different empirical discipline, and the places where the distinction itself stops being useful.

1. Two decisions, taken eleven days apart

On the morning of Thursday, 12 February 2026, Aparna Deshmukh, Chief Product Officer of Koshika Health Devices, sat in a conference room in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with two spreadsheets open and a decision she had been deferring since October. Koshika made a reusable adhesive patch, the Koshika Pulse, that read continuous heart rate, respiration rate and skin temperature and streamed them to a phone. It had shipped 214,000 units in eighteen months, almost all of them direct to consumers through Amazon India, Croma and the company's own storefront, at a maximum retail price of ₹5,499, with an optional ₹399-a-month app subscription that 31% of buyers attached. The business worked. It did not obviously grow.

The second spreadsheet described a different business with the same bill of materials. Over the previous year, three hospital groups and one diagnostics network had asked Koshika whether the patch could be used for post-discharge monitoring, with a clinician dashboard, escalation alerts, and integration into the hospital information system. One of them, a 700-bed group with four facilities in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, had put a number on paper: 250 devices at ₹7,900 each sold direct, a platform licence of ₹34 lakh a year, and ₹1.1 lakh of implementation. First-year contract value of ₹53.75 lakh; recurring value of ₹34 lakh. The sales cycle had run nine months so far and was not finished. Aparna's CFO, Meher Iyengar, had put a different number next to it: the hospital's standard payment terms were ninety days, sometimes a hundred and twenty; Koshika's contract manufacturer in Sriperumbudur wanted thirty days and worked on a twelve-week lead time. On the consumer side, marketplace settlement took fourteen days.

Eleven days later, on Monday, 23 February 2026, in a converted bungalow in Pune's Kalyani Nagar, Siddharth Venkataraman faced the mirror image of Aparna's problem. He was Chief Product Officer of Kovida Systems, which made an AI contract-intelligence product: upload a facility agreement, a vendor master services agreement or a lease, and Kovida extracted obligations, flagged deviations from a clause library, and produced a reviewer's summary. Kovida ran two motions from one codebase. Kovida Reader, sold self-serve at ₹1,499 per user per month, had 3,100 paying subscribers, mostly practising advocates, chartered accountants and two-person legal teams — a ₹5.6 crore annual run rate acquired almost entirely through search and word of mouth. Kovida Enterprise, sold to four banks and non-banking financial companies at an average annual contract value of ₹68 lakh, produced ₹2.72 crore. The enterprise line was smaller and, on every measure Siddharth's board looked at, better.

It was better for a reason that had nothing to do with the sales motion and everything to do with inference cost. Kovida spent roughly ₹3.80 in model and infrastructure cost for every page it processed. The median Reader subscriber processed 135 pages a month. The heaviest decile processed nine hundred. At ₹1,499 a month, a nine-hundred-page user cost Kovida ₹3,420 to serve and generated a gross margin of negative 128%. The enterprise customers, buying the identical capability, paid ₹52 lakh for a committed block of five lakh pages a year — ₹10.40 a page — against an internal alternative, junior-associate review at roughly ₹367 a page, that made the price look like a rounding error to them and a 63% gross margin to Kovida.

Both executives were facing what looks, at the level of the basic distinction, like the same question: should we go up-market, and what does it cost us? Both would have been badly served by the standard answer, which is that enterprise contracts are larger and therefore better. Aparna's enterprise opportunity was larger and, at Koshika's stage, more dangerous, because it consumed cash in a way the consumer business did not. Siddharth's enterprise line was structurally more profitable, but for a reason — usage-based pricing against a defensible internal comparator — that had nothing to do with the buyer being a business and everything to do with the pricing architecture the buyer's justification process permitted. The argument this page makes is that the B2B/B2C distinction is real, consequential, and almost always taught at the wrong level of abstraction: it is a proxy for four underlying variables, and once you can name and measure those four variables directly, the label stops doing useful work and occasionally does harmful work.

2. The idea, precisely stated, and the four schools that disagree about it

Begin with a definition that is tighter than the usual one. B2B versus B2C strategy is the study of how the structure of the buying decision — how many people must assent, whose money is at risk, whose career is at risk, and against what alternative the purchase is judged — determines the viable set of go-to-market motions, pricing architectures and product investments. On this definition, "business" and "consumer" are not categories of customer. They are names for two well-populated regions of a space whose dimensions are: (i) buyer–user distance, the number of people between the person with the problem and the person who signs; (ii) purchase reversibility, how cheaply the decision can be unwound; (iii) agency exposure, how much of the downside of a bad choice lands on the decider personally rather than on the entity; and (iv) comparator availability, whether the buyer has a costed internal alternative against which your price can be justified.

The idea was not invented to help product managers. It was invented to fix a defect in marketing theory. Through the 1950s, marketing was consumer marketing; industrial selling was treated as a species of personal salesmanship, not a discipline with its own behavioural model. Theodore Levitt's Marketing Myopia (1960) had shifted attention from products to customer needs, but it did not distinguish between a customer who was a household and a customer who was a procurement department. The correction came from two directions. In 1967, Patrick Robinson, Charles Faris and Yoram Wind published the BUYGRID framework, which introduced buyclasses — new task, modified rebuy, straight rebuy — and made the obvious but then-unstated point that a first-time purchase and a renewal are different decisions with different participants. Five years later, Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind's Organizational Buying Behavior (1972) named the buying center and its roles: initiator, user, influencer, decider, buyer, gatekeeper. Jagdish Sheth's 1973 model of industrial buying behaviour added the psychology: purchasing agents, engineers and users arrive with systematically different information sources, different risk tolerances and different definitions of a good outcome, and the purchase is the resolution of that conflict rather than the expression of a single preference.

Underneath all of this sits an economic argument that practitioners rarely make explicit but that explains most of what they observe. Ronald Coase's 1937 question — why do firms exist? — and Oliver Williamson's later work on transaction-cost economics establish that organisations govern exchange by contract precisely where asset specificity and hold-up risk are high. That is why B2B purchases come wrapped in master service agreements, uptime credits and data-processing addenda: the contract is not bureaucratic residue, it is the governance mechanism that makes the transaction possible at all. Michael Jensen and William Meckling's 1976 agency framework supplies the second half: the person signing is an agent spending a principal's money, and agents optimise for a different objective function than principals do. Add Kahneman and Tversky's finding that losses are weighted roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains, and you can predict most enterprise buying behaviour from first principles: a buying committee is a loss-averse agent, and everything it does — pilots, references, certifications, phased rollouts, incumbent preference — is variance reduction, not value maximisation.

That framing has been contested for fifty years, and the disagreements are live. Four schools are worth being able to represent faithfully, because a competent practitioner will invoke one of them at you and you will need to know which proposition they are actually committed to.

The synthesis usually offered — "it's a spectrum, use judgement" — is true and nearly useless, because it does not tell you which variable to measure. The rest of this page takes the harder path: making the four underlying variables quantitative, working out what follows, and being explicit about where the evidence runs out.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic practitioners leave implicit

3.1 The approval cascade, and why certification is a pricing decision

The most useful piece of formal machinery in this topic is also the simplest. Model a business sale as a series of independent gates, each with a probability of passage. If a deal must survive n approvers and the probability that approver i assents is pi, the unconditional close probability is the product of the pi. The independence assumption is wrong in detail — approvers talk, and a strong champion raises everyone's p — but it is wrong in a direction that makes the model conservative and the conclusions robust.

Take Kovida's enterprise pipeline as Siddharth actually mapped it in January 2026, after losing two deals at what his team had recorded as "late stage". Six gates: the champion in the legal operations team (0.90), the department head who owns the budget (0.88), the information-security reviewer (0.62), the data-protection officer and legal (0.80), procurement (0.85), and the chief financial officer, whose sign-off was required above the bank's ₹25 lakh delegated-authority threshold (0.75). The product of those six numbers is 0.250. A pipeline that felt, deal by deal, like a series of near-misses was in fact converting exactly as the arithmetic predicted.

Figure 1. The single lowest gate dominates the product. Raising the information-security gate from 0.62 to 0.95 — the effect Kovida measured across its next eleven deals after completing a SOC 2 Type II audit and publishing a data-processing addendum aligned to India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — lifts the close rate by 13.4 percentage points, a 53% relative improvement, without changing the product's function at all. Removing the CFO gate entirely by pricing the entry package below the bank's ₹25 lakh delegated-authority threshold lifts it further, to 51.2%.

Three consequences follow, and all three are counter-intuitive to a practitioner trained on consumer products. The first is that the binding constraint is the minimum gate, not the average one. Kovida's team had spent two quarters improving demonstration quality, which raised the champion's p from an already-high 0.86 to 0.90 and moved the close rate by about one point. Nine weeks of security-audit work moved it by thirteen. The second is that reducing n is a legitimate product and pricing strategy. The entry package that Siddharth eventually shipped — a single-workflow licence at ₹19.8 lakh, deliberately set below the ₹25 lakh threshold at which most of his target banks escalate to a purchase committee — was not a discount. It was a structural removal of a 0.75 multiplier. The third is that in consumer businesses this entire apparatus collapses to n = 1, which is why consumer product teams can afford to think about persuasion and habit and almost never about veto.

3.2 The buyer's objective function is not the firm's

The second piece of machinery explains why pilots exist. A consumer buying the Koshika Pulse performs an approximately straightforward calculation: perceived annual value, say ₹1,800 in reassurance and better sleep data, against a price of ₹5,499 amortised over an expected two years of use plus ₹399 a month if they attach the subscription. They may be wrong about the value, and they are certainly influenced by framing, but the objective function is their own, the money is their own, and the decision is reversible within the marketplace's return window.

A hospital's clinical-operations head evaluating Koshika Clinic performs a different calculation, and the difference is not sophistication — it is that a term appears which has no consumer analogue. Call the expected organisational value V, the probability that the deployment fails visibly q, and the personal cost to the decider of a visible failure C, weighted by a loss-aversion coefficient λ of roughly 2.25. The decider's private expected value is approximately (1 − q)·V − λ·q·C. With V = ₹40 lakh of avoided readmission cost and nursing time, q = 0.20 for an unproven vendor, and C = ₹25 lakh in reputational terms, the calculation runs 0.80 × 40 − 2.25 × 0.20 × 25 = 32 − 11.25 = ₹20.75 lakh. Positive, but not compellingly so relative to the effort of championing it. Run a three-month, one-ward pilot that drops q to 0.05, and the same deal is worth 0.95 × 40 − 2.25 × 0.05 × 25 = 38 − 2.8 = ₹35.2 lakh to the same person. The deal did not get better. The variance got smaller, and variance is what the agent is actually paid to manage.

Figure 2. The same contract, valued by a consumer-style calculation and by an agent's calculation. The pilot adds no capability and costs Koshika nine weeks of deployment engineering; it raises the decider's private expected value by ₹14.45 lakh, a 70% improvement, purely by reducing the probability of visible failure. This is why free trials do different work in the two worlds: in consumer they are price and value discovery, in enterprise they are insurance.

This reframing has a sharp practical corollary that separates practitioners. If the enterprise buyer's binding term is λ·q·C, then a large share of what gets called "enterprise features" are not features at all. Single sign-on, SCIM user provisioning, immutable audit logs, role-based access control, data-residency guarantees, uptime credits, a signed data-processing addendum, an independent penetration-test report: none of these do work the user values, and almost none of them appear in usage analytics. They exist to drive q down and to give the champion something to hand a reviewer. Teams that score these on a standard reach-impact-confidence-effort grid will systematically under-prioritise them, because the grid measures value to users and these items produce value to the decision.

3.3 Where the revenue comes from, and why expansion is structurally asymmetric

The third piece of machinery is distributional. In a consumer subscription business, revenue per customer is bounded above by the price, so the revenue distribution across customers is close to uniform and its variance comes almost entirely from tenure. In a business with organisational customers, revenue per account is set by the size of the organisation, and organisation size follows a power law. Koshika's consumer business earned between ₹0 and about ₹8,500 from every buyer. Kotwal Compliance Cloud, a Bengaluru company selling transaction monitoring and regulatory reporting to non-banking financial companies, earned ₹4.1 lakh from its smallest customer and ₹2.9 crore from its largest.

Figure 3. In the consumer business the top decile of customers produces 13% of revenue; in the contract business it produces 41%, and the top three deciles produce 70%. The consequence is not merely that account management matters more. It is that the two businesses require different governance: a consumer business can be run on averages and cohort curves, a contract business cannot, because its average is not a fact about any customer.

The asymmetry that matters more, and that is under-taught, concerns expansion. An organisation that buys your product can buy more of it next year without your acquiring anything: it hires people, it grows its loan book, a regulator publishes a circular that creates a new reporting obligation. A consumer cannot. A household does not acquire more households. Net revenue retention — the revenue this year from last year's cohort, including upsell and downgrade, divided by last year's revenue from that cohort — can therefore exceed 100% structurally in B2B and only exceptionally in B2C, and the compounding difference over a few years is enormous.

3.4 The low-sample-size problem

The last piece of mechanics is methodological, and it is the one that most clearly makes B2B product management a different empirical discipline rather than the same discipline with longer sales cycles. Consider the sample size needed to detect a 10% relative improvement on a 20% baseline conversion rate at conventional thresholds — 5% significance, 80% power. The standard approximation, n ≈ 16·p(1−p)/δ², gives 16 × 0.16 / 0.0004 ≈ 6,400 users per arm. Koshika's consumer app, with 214,000 installed devices and roughly 66,000 monthly actives, can run that experiment in ten days and run sixteen of them a quarter. Kovida Reader, with 3,100 subscribers, cannot power a single arm of it. Kovida Enterprise, with four customers, is not in the same universe of inference.

The honest conclusion is not that B2B teams should run underpowered tests and quote the p-values anyway, which is common and corrosive. It is that B2B product management must rest on a different evidential base: structured win/loss interviews where n = 20 is a large study, instrumented traces of individual accounts read like clinical case notes, close analysis of the exact language in which a champion justified the purchase internally, and pre-registered qualitative predictions ("if this hypothesis is right, the security reviewer at the next two banks will ask about model training data before they ask about encryption"). Siddharth's team kept what they called a deal autopsy file: for every loss, a one-page record of which gate failed, the sentence in which the objection was first raised, and whether anyone at Kovida had heard that sentence before. After eleven deals it was a better predictive instrument than any dashboard they had, and it would have been statistically worthless as a sample.

4. When the distinction applies, and when it actively misleads

The distinction earns its keep under four testable conditions. State them as claims that can be checked against a real company rather than as characteristics.

Claim one: buyer–user distance is greater than zero. Check by counting the named individuals between the person who feels the problem and the person whose signature releases money. For Koshika's consumer business the count is zero: the person with palpitations buys the patch. For Koshika Clinic the count is four, and one of them — the hospital's information-security officer, who has never treated a patient — can veto on grounds that have nothing to do with clinical value. Where the count is zero the entire apparatus of champions, gates and internal justification is dead weight, and importing it produces the familiar pathology of a consumer company that builds an admin console nobody asked for.

Claim two: the buyer has a costed internal comparator. Check by asking what the buyer does today and what it costs them per unit. Kovida's bank comparator is junior-associate review at ₹367 a page; this is why ₹10.40 a page is defensible and why a per-seat price would have been a strategic error, since seats have no comparator and pages do. Koshika's consumer buyer has no costed comparator for "knowing my resting heart rate", which is why consumer pricing is anchored psychologically — against a fitness band at ₹3,499 or a monthly streaming subscription at ₹149 — rather than against a computed alternative. Where no comparator exists, value-based pricing is theatre.

Claim three: the decision is irreversible enough to be worth insuring. Check by asking what it costs the buyer to switch away in year two. A consumer uninstalls. A hospital that has put Koshika Clinic into its discharge protocol, trained two hundred nurses and integrated with its information system has a switching cost in the tens of lakhs, which is why it will spend nine months de-risking the entry decision. Where switching is cheap, long sales cycles are not caution but friction, and a company that adds procurement theatre to a low-switching-cost product is simply slower than its competitors for no compensating benefit.

Claim four: revenue per customer is dispersed enough that averages mislead. Check the ratio of the largest customer's revenue to the median customer's. Below roughly 5:1, run the business on averages. Above roughly 20:1, averages are actively dangerous and the company needs per-account governance. Kotwal's ratio was 71:1.

Now the cases where the distinction misleads, which matter more because they are where competent practitioners go wrong. The first is self-serve small-business software, where the buyer is legally a business and behaves in every operational respect like a consumer: one person, own money in practice, card payment, no procurement, decision in minutes. Tally Solutions built a very large business in India on buyers who are firms and decisions that are individual. Labelling this "B2B" and staffing it with a field sales team destroys the economics, because the contract value cannot support a human being in the loop. The second is prosumer, which the basic treatment usually flags but rarely quantifies: the tell is that the buyer wants consumer-grade signup speed and enterprise-grade record-keeping, and the cost of serving that combination is that you build audit trails for customers who will never pay an enterprise price for them. The third, and the most expensive, is the assumption that going up-market is a go-to-market change. It is usually a product change, an organisational change and a balance-sheet change, and section 8 contains a case where a competent team got all three wrong.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

Multi-product companies and the second-product problem

Once a company sells two products, the B2B/B2C question must be asked per product and per motion, and the answers frequently conflict. Koshika's two products shared a sensor, a firmware team and a data pipeline, and diverged completely above that line. The seam showed up in an unglamorous place: the firmware release train. Consumer devices could take an over-the-air update on a Tuesday; hospital devices were inside a validated clinical workflow and could not be updated without a change-control process and, for some modifications, a fresh conformity assessment under the Medical Devices Rules. For eleven months Koshika ran one release train, which meant the consumer product shipped at the clinical product's cadence — one release every nine weeks instead of every fortnight. Nobody decided this. It was the residue of a shared repository and a shared release manager.

Two-sided marketplaces

A marketplace does not have a B2B side and a B2C side so much as two independent buying structures that happen to share a ledger. Kosal Agri Networks, which connects farmer producer organisations in Vidarbha and Marathwada with institutional buyers — hotel groups, quick-commerce warehouses, two national retail chains — carried 2,400 supply-side accounts and 180 demand-side accounts against ₹310 crore of gross merchandise value at a 6.5% take rate. Each demand-side account was therefore worth ₹1.72 crore of GMV and received named account management with quarterly business reviews; each supply-side account cost ₹340 to onboard through a field agent and was served by a vernacular mobile app with no human in the loop. Both sides are businesses. Neither is "B2B" in the sense that determines a playbook. The variable that determined the motion was concentration, exactly as the four conditions in section 4 predict.

Regulated products

Regulation does something interesting to the distinction: it collapses it on the compliance axis and widens it on the liability axis. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's requirements for a Class B medical device apply to Koshika whether the patch is bought by a patient on a marketplace or by a hospital on a purchase order; the regulator is a silent participant in both purchases. But the liability structures diverge sharply. A consumer claim is small, individual and handled under consumer protection law; a hospital contract carries indemnities, service credits and, in one of Koshika's draft agreements, a clause making Koshika liable for clinical consequences of a missed alert. Meher Iyengar's objection in the February meeting was not about the revenue. It was that a ₹34 lakh contract carried an indemnity cap of ₹2 crore.

Artificial-intelligence products break one of the assumptions that quietly underpinned two decades of software strategy: that marginal cost is near zero, gross margins sit near 80%, and therefore a flat subscription price is safe. 6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The unit of analysis is the purchase, not the customer. A competent practitioner segments customers; an expert segments purchases, because the same organisation buys differently on different occasions. A bank buying Kovida's first workflow licence is running a new-task purchase with six gates; the same bank adding a second workflow eleven months later is running a modified rebuy with two. The tell in the wild: a company whose sales cycle data shows a bimodal distribution — a cluster at three weeks and a cluster at seven months — and which reports the mean. The obvious reading, that the sales team is inconsistent, is wrong; the two clusters are two different purchase types and should have two different processes.

Buyer–user distance predicts more than the label does. A competent practitioner asks whether the customer is a business. An expert asks how many people sit between the person who has the problem and the person who signs, and treats that integer as the primary design input. The tell: when you ask a product manager who their user is and they answer with a job title rather than a name, and then cannot tell you who in that person's organisation can say no. The obvious reading is that they need better personas. They need a different question.

A large share of the enterprise roadmap is evidence production, not capability. Experts recognise that some features exist so a champion can show something to somebody: the exportable return-on-investment summary, the quarterly business review deck generator, the compliance attestation page. These have near-zero daily usage and high renewal impact. The tell: a feature with sub-2% monthly active usage that appears in every renewal conversation. The obvious reading — low usage, deprecate it — is exactly backwards, and deprecating it is how companies discover what it was for.

Consumer churn is a rate; enterprise churn is an event. Rates are managed statistically, with cohort curves and interventions tested on thousands. Events are managed narratively: you can name each one, and each has a cause you could have known. The tell: whether the team can recite the reason for every one of last year's lost accounts. If they can, they are running an event discipline. If they say "churn was 9%", on a base of forty customers, they are applying consumer methods to a population where averages have no referent.

Low sample size changes the method, not just the confidence interval. The expert response to four enterprise customers is not to run a test with four customers; it is to switch to mechanistic reasoning, pre-registered qualitative predictions, and close reading of individual cases. The tell: an experiment write-up in a B2B company that reports a percentage lift without reporting n. The obvious reading is sloppiness. The real problem is that the team has not noticed it is in a different epistemic regime and is spending months generating numbers that cannot inform a decision.

Most of your business market is not buying, and the consumer marketing discipline applies more than B2B practitioners admit. If the average replacement cycle for a category is four years, roughly 5% of the market is in-market in any given quarter. Kotwal's addressable market was about 1,100 regulated entities, so roughly 55 were in-market at a time, against a pipeline covering 22. The other 1,045 were not prospects; they were future prospects whose memory of the category is being formed now. The tell: a B2B company that measures all marketing on last-touch attribution to pipeline and cannot explain why its win rate is higher in the two cities where it has sponsored an industry conference for three years. The obvious reading — the conference generates leads — is usually wrong; it generates recall, which shows up as a higher p at the first gate eighteen months later.

Price in business markets is set against the buyer's justification narrative, not their willingness to pay. The enterprise buyer must be able to state, in one sentence to a superior, why this price is right. That sentence needs a comparator and a unit. "₹10.40 a page against ₹367 for a junior associate" is such a sentence; "₹1,499 per seat" is not, because the superior's next question is how many seats and why. The tell: a deal that stalls after a verbal yes, at the stage where the champion has to write the note. The obvious reading is procurement delay. The actual problem is that you have not given your champion a sentence.

Expansion revenue is structurally available on one side of the line and structurally scarce on the other. An expert knows that a consumer subscription business must eventually become a pricing-and-portfolio business because it cannot grow within an account, and plans the second SKU years before it is needed. The tell: a consumer company celebrating flat net revenue retention of 98% as if it were the same achievement as a business company's 98%, which would be a crisis. The obvious reading treats the metric as comparable across contexts. It is not.

In India, the tax and payments plumbing shifts the effective price between the two buyers. A GST-registered business buying a ₹10 lakh annual contract recovers the ₹1.8 lakh of goods-and-services tax as input credit; a consumer paying ₹11,800 for a ₹10,000 service bears the whole ₹1,800. The same list price is therefore about 18% cheaper in real terms to the business buyer, which is one reason prosumer pricing sits awkwardly. On the collection side, the Reserve Bank's e-mandate framework, with its additional-factor authentication and pre-debit notification requirements, makes recurring consumer collection genuinely lossy: Koshika measured 3.1% monthly involuntary churn on its ₹399 subscription from mandate failures alone, roughly 40% of total churn. The tell: a consumer subscription whose churn spikes on the same days each month. The obvious reading is a product problem; it is a payments problem, and it is usually the cheapest churn a team will ever fix.

The seam, not the strategy, is where dual-motion companies fail. Experts spend disproportionate attention on the handover: who owns an account at ₹8 lakh, what happens to the inside representative's commission when a self-serve account is later claimed by the field team, whether the self-serve product is allowed to show a price the field team must then defend. The tell: the number of accounts disputed between teams in a quarter, a number nobody reports and everybody knows. The obvious reading is that this is a sales-operations problem below the product manager's altitude. It determines which customers get which product experience, which makes it a product decision that the product organisation has declined to make.

Certification and compliance artefacts are priced assets, not costs. A SOC 2 Type II report, an ISO 27001 certificate, a completed CERT-In incident-reporting posture, a DPDP-aligned data-processing addendum: each raises a specific gate's probability, and the increment is measurable if the company keeps gate-level loss data. Kovida's audit cost ₹34 lakh and nine weeks; on a pipeline of thirty deals a year at ₹68 lakh average, a 13.4-point close-rate improvement is worth ₹2.7 crore of annual contract value. The tell: a company that books certification under general and administrative expenses and never computes its return. The obvious reading is that compliance is overhead. It is the highest-return product work available to most early enterprise companies, and it does not look like product work at all.

7. How this differs by product type and by company stage

In pure consumer products the distinctive discipline is statistical: large samples, cohort curves, habit loops, and a marketing organisation that is really an experimentation organisation. The scarce resource is attention, the binding metric is retention at day 30 and day 90, and the most common strategic error is over-investing in acquisition when retention is the higher-leverage lever. In B2B and enterprise products the distinctive discipline is political and evidentiary: mapping buying centres, producing artefacts that reduce perceived variance, and managing a small number of accounts as individual cases. The scarce resource is credibility, the binding metric is net revenue retention, and the most common error is mistaking a signed pilot for proof of a repeatable motion.

In platforms and marketplaces the honest statement is that the label does not apply at the company level at all; it applies per side, and the determinant is concentration rather than legal customer type, as Kosal Agri Networks demonstrates with a field-force motion on one side and key accounts on the other. In hardware and physical goods the distinction acquires a balance-sheet dimension that pure software people consistently underestimate: channel margin and returns on the consumer side, payment terms and inventory on the business side, and a cash-conversion cycle that can make the more profitable business the less survivable one. In AI-native products the distinction sharpens rather than dissolves, because the pricing architectures that the two buyers will accept — flat for consumers, metered for businesses — have opposite relationships to a cost base that now scales with usage.

Stage changes which of these is binding. At pre-product-market-fit the distinction barely matters; what matters is finding anyone with an urgent problem and the authority to act on it, which in practice biases early companies toward whichever buyer can say yes fastest, and that bias is usually correct. At the first-scaling stage, roughly ₹5 to ₹50 crore of revenue, the distinction becomes the single most consequential organisational fact, because it determines whether you are hiring sales engineers or growth engineers, and those are not fungible. At scale, most successful companies run both motions and the question becomes governance: separate profit-and-loss statements, separate metrics, separate release cadences where the products genuinely differ, and an explicit written rule for the seam. Where the difference is not real, say so plainly: the engineering practices, the discovery methods for understanding a user's actual workflow, and the discipline of writing down what you will not build are the same on both sides of the line, and treating them as different is a common way for companies to maintain two mediocre product cultures instead of one good one.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Kotwal Compliance Cloud: getting the metric right, and paying a tax for it

Kotwal sold regulatory reporting and transaction monitoring to forty-one non-banking financial companies and small banks, at ₹18.6 crore of annual recurring revenue and an average contract of ₹45.4 lakh. Its founders made one decision in 2022 that determined everything afterwards: they priced on monitored accounts rather than on user seats. The consequence was that when a customer's loan book grew 30%, Kotwal's revenue from that customer grew with it, without a salesperson, a negotiation or a renewal event. That alone produced about 26 points of the company's 39% gross expansion. Add modules triggered by regulatory change — each new Reserve Bank circular that created a reporting obligation was, to Kotwal, a product launch with pre-committed demand — and net revenue retention reached 128%.

The cost appeared on the engineering side. In the financial year 2025, 38% of Kotwal's engineering capacity went to contractual commitments made during sales cycles: bespoke report formats, integrations with three different core banking systems, and one customer's insistence on an on-premises deployment. Worse, when the head of engineering finally instrumented it, six of the forty-one customers accounted for 44% of the commitment load while producing 19% of revenue. The remedy was not to fire them; it was to introduce a rule that no commitment could be made in a sales cycle without a written note explaining how it would generalise to at least three other customers, and to move the on-premises customer to a higher price tier that funded a dedicated pod. The roadmap tax fell to 22% over four quarters. The generalisable lesson is that in business markets, the roadmap is a second currency that the sales organisation spends without seeing the balance.

Kopal Payments: when the buyer is a business but the metric is a consumer metric

Kopal Payments, in Chennai, sold a lending and collections stack to 140 non-banking financial companies whose own customers were retail borrowers. Its buyer was a risk-and-compliance committee. Its user was a borrower on a phone at eleven at night, and whether the contract renewed depended almost entirely on whether that borrower finished the application. For three years Kopal priced per seat for the lender's operations staff — a metric with no relationship to the value it created — and its product organisation prioritised the operations console, which the buyer saw, over the borrower journey, which the buyer did not.

The repricing in 2025 changed both. Kopal moved to ₹38 per successful disbursal. Immediately, the revenue line and the borrower funnel became the same object. A four-point improvement in borrower completion, from 61% to 65%, across one client's 80,000 monthly applications meant 3,200 additional disbursals, worth roughly ₹59 lakh a month to the client at their unit economics and ₹1.22 lakh a month to Kopal. Across the base, revenue rose from ₹6.2 crore to ₹9.8 crore in three quarters with no new customers. The roadmap reoriented toward consumer-grade funnel work — vernacular error messages, a re-entry flow for dropped applications, a document-upload step rebuilt for low-bandwidth connections — which the previous pricing model had made invisible. This is the cleanest available demonstration that in B2B2C, the pricing metric decides which of your two users the product organisation actually serves.

Koyal Audio: a competent team, a correct-sounding pivot, and eighteen months lost

Koyal Audio, founded in Mumbai in 2020, ran a consumer audio-stories and podcast app with 1.9 million monthly active users and 61,000 paying subscribers at ₹149 a month — ₹90.9 lakh of monthly recurring revenue, about ₹10.9 crore annualised. By mid-2024 subscriber growth had fallen to 2% a month and advertising revenue was thin. The board reached the conclusion that many boards reach: consumer is hard, enterprise pays better, and the company should sell to businesses.

The resulting product, Koyal for Work, delivered audio briefings for internal communications at large employers: leadership updates, safety briefings and compliance training rendered as listenable audio in nine languages. It was a defensible-sounding idea. The company spent eighteen months and about ₹11 crore on it, hired six enterprise sales people, ran nine pilots and converted two, worth ₹96 lakh of combined annual value. Both churned at first renewal.

The post-mortem identified four causes, in increasing order of importance. First, the sales cycle was nine to fourteen months against a plan of four, which meant the cash model was wrong from week one. Second, the buying centre was diffuse: internal communications sat under corporate affairs, the budget sat with human resources operations, and human resources operations already bought a learning management system that they considered the incumbent. Third, and decisively, internal communications had no budget line. Koyal had found a real problem attached to no money — the single most reliable way to lose a year in business markets. Fourth, the organisational cost: Koyal's four strongest engineers moved to the enterprise track, and consumer day-30 retention fell from 41% to 29% over the same period while monthly recurring revenue on the consumer side fell from ₹90.9 lakh to ₹61 lakh. Runway went from twenty-six months to seven.

The recovery is more instructive than the failure. In late 2025 the founders asked a question they had not asked in 2024: not "which customer type pays more" but "which buyer has an existing budget line for the asset we actually own." Koyal's defensible asset was not a podcast app. It was a rights-cleared library of regional-language voice talent and a synthesis stack that produced natural Marathi, Bengali, Tamil and Bhojpuri speech at low cost. The buyers with a budget line for that were product teams at consumer-facing businesses: an education company that needed lesson audio in seven languages, a bank modernising its interactive voice response, a news publisher producing audio editions. Koyal relaunched as a B2B2C rendering interface priced at ₹0.42 a minute of audio generated. By the third quarter of 2026 that line produced ₹7.4 crore of annual recurring revenue across four accounts at 72% gross margin. The consumer app was kept alive, deliberately, as a demonstration surface and a talent-relationship asset rather than as the business. Recovery took fourteen months and a 40% reduction in headcount, and the thing that made it possible was that the new buyer was a product team — a buying centre of two people with a usage-metered budget and an existing vendor line — rather than a communications department with none.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs, and the cost of late detection

Selling to a problem with no budget line. The early warning sign is enthusiasm without escalation: champions who love the demonstration, attend every call, and never introduce anyone senior. The diagnostic question is "what budget does this come out of this year, and who owns it?" — asked in the second meeting, not the sixth. The cost of catching it late is the whole cycle: Koyal lost eighteen months and ₹11 crore to this one failure mode.

Mistaking a pilot for a motion. The warning sign is a pipeline in which every deal is the founder's deal. The diagnostic question is whether any contract has closed without a founder in the room, and whether any has renewed. The cost of catching it late is a sales team hired against an unrepeatable playbook, which typically shows up nine months later as three departures and a quarter of missed quota.

Blended-metric blindness. When a company reports a single customer acquisition cost across two motions, it conceals both. A blended figure of, say, ₹9,400 might be ₹1,750 on the consumer side and ₹22 lakh on the enterprise side, and no decision can be made on the blend. The warning sign is a board deck with one funnel chart. The diagnostic question is "show me this metric split by motion, and if you cannot, why not?" The cost of catching it late is capital allocated to the wrong motion for a year.

Roadmap capture by the largest account. The warning sign is a quarterly plan in which more than a quarter of engineering capacity is traceable to named-customer commitments. The diagnostic question, borrowed from Kotwal, is "which other three customers will use this?" The cost of catching it late is a product that is a bespoke system for two customers, priced as if it were a product, with the margin structure of a services firm.

Importing a consumer engagement metric into a business product. The warning sign is a product manager worrying about low daily active usage on a tool that is correctly used once a fortnight. The diagnostic question is whether the paying buyer has ever mentioned the metric you are optimising. The cost of catching it late is a year of engagement features on a product whose renewal depends on audit completeness.

Ignoring the lowest gate. The warning sign is a consistent cluster of losses at one stage, usually recorded in the customer relationship system with a vague reason code. The diagnostic question is gate-level: "for each of the last ten losses, which named individual's objection ended it?" The cost of catching it late is measurable — for Kovida, two quarters of pipeline at a 25% close rate instead of 38%, which on a thirty-deal year is about ₹2.7 crore of annual contract value not signed.

Under-pricing the compliance and security work. The warning sign is a security questionnaire being answered ad hoc by an engineer at eleven at night for the fourth time. The diagnostic question is how many engineering hours went into questionnaires last quarter and what a certification would have cost instead. The cost of catching it late is both the lost deals and the opportunity cost of senior engineering time spent on a problem with a purchasable solution.

Letting the working-capital cycle grow unnoticed. The warning sign is revenue growth with flat or falling bank balance and rising receivables — the exact pattern Meher Iyengar flagged at Koshika. The diagnostic question is "what is our cash conversion cycle by motion, and how much cash does the next ₹1 crore of enterprise revenue consume?" The cost of catching it late is the most expensive of all, because it is discovered when payroll is three weeks out and the remedy — discounting for advance payment, or emergency debt — is taken from a position of no leverage.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether business buying is more like consumer buying than practitioners believe. The Ehrenberg-Bass position, steelmanned, is this: the empirical laws that describe consumer markets — double jeopardy, the dominance of light buyers, the primacy of mental and physical availability — have been replicated in business categories, and the elaborate rationalist picture of the buying committee is a story practitioners tell because it flatters their profession. If only 5% of buyers are in-market at any time, then the dominant determinant of who wins is which brands are recalled when the need arises, which is a memory-encoding problem solved by broad, distinctive, long-running advertising, not by targeting. The evidence is a substantial body of replicated purchase-panel work and the Binet and Field finding that long-term brand investment outperforms short-term activation in business categories too, at roughly a 46:54 split rather than consumer's 60:40. The opposing position, steelmanned, is that these laws describe categories with many buyers and frequent repeat purchase, and that the categories where most enterprise software actually lives — a few hundred possible customers, a four-year cycle, a six-person committee, and a price that requires board attention — violate the conditions the laws were derived under. What would have to be true for each to be wrong: the Ehrenberg-Bass position fails if measured recall among out-market buyers does not predict inclusion in the eventual consideration set in concentrated categories; the buying-centre position fails if gate-level interventions stop predicting close rates once brand recall is controlled for. Almost nobody runs the study, because it requires a company to spend money on brand advertising for three years and instrument it honestly.

Whether product-led growth has a ceiling. The optimistic position holds that the ceiling keeps rising: bottom-up adoption created companies that reached very large enterprise revenue with a fraction of the historic sales cost, and each year more of the buying committee's objections become self-serviceable through published compliance posture, in-product administrative controls and transparent pricing. The pessimistic position, argued most sharply by practitioners who have run both, is that above a certain contract value a human being closes the deal, not because software cannot explain itself but because the buyer requires a counterparty who can be held responsible. On this reading, self-serve motions do not scale into enterprise; they generate the demand that a sales team then converts, and calling that "product-led" obscures the fact that the expensive part is still expensive. What would settle it: the distribution of contract values closed with no human contact, tracked over a decade, in categories with genuine security review. The available evidence is contaminated because the companies that publish it have an interest in the answer.

Whether a company should ever run both motions. The focus school argues that a company has one culture, one set of instincts, one hiring filter, and that dual motions produce two half-organisations that each lose to a competitor doing only one thing; the evidence is the long list of consumer companies that destroyed themselves reaching for enterprise revenue, of which Koyal is a small instance. The portfolio school argues that the underlying asset — a model, a sensor, a network — is frequently monetisable through two buyers with different price elasticities, and that refusing the second buyer forfeits the return on an asset already paid for; the evidence is Koshika, where the same sensor earns 43% margin from one buyer and 72% from another. What would have to be true: the focus school is wrong if companies running dual motions with separate profit-and-loss statements, separate release trains and an explicit seam rule show no deterioration in either motion's metrics. Nobody has published that comparison with adequate controls, and selection effects are severe, since only companies doing well enough to afford two motions attempt them.

Whether the distinction should be retired in favour of purchase complexity. A growing minority argues that "B2B" and "B2C" are legacy vocabulary inherited from how sales forces were organised in the 1970s, and that the field should speak instead of contract-value bands and approval-chain depth, which are measurable and which predict the operating model directly. The counter-argument is not that the replacement is wrong but that the label carries real information the replacement loses: tax treatment, liability structure, the applicable consumer-protection regime, the payments plumbing, and the fact that an organisation persists and grows while a household does not. The honest position: the label is a lossy compression of four variables, and the disagreement is about whether the compression is lossy enough to be harmful. This page has taken the view that it is harmful at the level of operating decisions and useful at the level of legal and financial structure, which is not a synthesis anyone would call elegant.

Whether AI-native products collapse the distinction. One camp argues that when the same model serves a consumer and an enterprise, the marginal product is identical and only the wrapper differs, so the distinction becomes purely commercial. The other argues the opposite — that AI widens the gap, because the acceptable error rate, the evidentiary burden, the data-governance requirement and the pricing architecture diverge more sharply than they ever did in deterministic software: a consumer tolerates a wrong answer and reruns the prompt, while a bank cannot, and the work required to move from tolerable to auditable is most of the engineering. The evidence so far is thin and mostly anecdotal in both directions, which is a reason to hold the question open rather than to pick the position that matches one's existing commitments.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can describe the differences between the two motions fluently and will reach for the spectrum metaphor when pressed. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

First, they ask about structure before they ask about category. Presented with a new business, their first three questions are how many people must say yes, what the buyer does today and what it costs them, and how concentrated the revenue is — not whether the customer is a business. They can then predict the operating model, and they are usually right.

Second, they treat the seam as their responsibility. They will have an opinion, in writing, about which accounts belong to which motion, what happens at the boundary, and how a person is compensated when an account crosses it, and they will recognise that declining to have that opinion does not make the question go away; it delegates it to whoever shouts loudest in the weekly pipeline meeting.

Third, they are fluent in the arithmetic without being ruled by it. They can compute a close-rate cascade, a working-capital requirement and a margin-by-usage-decile table on a whiteboard, and they also know that the decisive input is often a number nobody has yet — a renewal that has not happened, a churn rate with no observations — and they will say so out loud rather than presenting an assumption in the costume of a forecast.

Fourth, they hold the distinction lightly at the level of practice and firmly at the level of structure. They do not run consumer growth experiments on four enterprise accounts, and they do not build a buying-committee apparatus for a product one person buys in four minutes; but they also do not let the label stop them from noticing that their small-business self-serve customers are behaving exactly like consumers, that their prosumer segment wants two incompatible things, or that their most profitable product line is the one their category vocabulary has no name for.

12. What Aparna and Siddharth decided

Aparna Deshmukh's recommendation to the Koshika board on 3 March 2026 was to take the hospital contract and to cap the enterprise motion at three accounts for eighteen months. Her reasoning was almost entirely the working-capital row in Table 3 rather than the margin row: the clinical business was more profitable per unit and consumed ₹1.49 crore more cash per ₹4 crore of revenue, and Koshika had ₹9 crore in the bank. She negotiated two structural terms that mattered more than the price — 40% of the first-year value payable on delivery rather than on acceptance, and a separate purchase order for hardware so that inventory was not financed against a software milestone — and she split the release train, accepting a permanent duplication of two engineers' effort in exchange for letting the consumer product ship fortnightly again. She also declined the indemnity structure and lost six weeks re-negotiating it, which she judged correctly to be cheaper than the alternative.

Siddharth Venkataraman's decision at Kovida was to keep both motions and to change what each was for. Kovida Reader was reclassified, explicitly and in writing, from a revenue line to a demand-generation and model-improvement asset: it would be priced to a 65% gross margin after the routing work, with a fair-use ceiling at 400 pages and metered overage beyond it, and its primary success metric became qualified enterprise pipeline sourced from Reader accounts rather than Reader revenue. Kovida Enterprise got the ₹19.8 lakh single-workflow entry package priced below the delegated-authority threshold, the SOC 2 Type II audit, and a rule that no security questionnaire would be answered by an engineer more than once before the answer went into a published trust page. He did not resolve the seam. Fourteen accounts remained disputed at the end of the quarter, and he wrote in his own planning document that this was the part of the plan he was least confident about.

Discussion questions

  1. Aparna justified her decision on the cash-conversion cycle rather than on gross margin. Was she right to weight a balance-sheet constraint above a profit-and-loss advantage, and under what conditions — of capital availability, of competitive urgency, of customer concentration — would the same analysis have produced the opposite recommendation?
  2. Siddharth repositioned a profitable consumer line as a demand-generation asset for an enterprise line. Identify the assumptions on which that reclassification depends. If Reader's subscribers turn out not to be employed at the banks Kovida sells to, what has he actually given up, and how quickly would he know?
  3. Koyal Audio's recovery came from asking which buyer had a budget line for the asset the company already owned, rather than which customer type paid more. Apply that question to Koshika and to Kovida. Does it change either decision, and if it does not, what does that tell you about the generality of the lesson?

13. Going deeper

The product strategy document
The place where the four variables in section 2 either get written down or get left implicit. Writing the buyer structure into the strategy document is what converts this analysis from an insight into a constraint the organisation is accountable to.
B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction
The foundation this page assumes. Worth revisiting once to check that the buyer–user split, sales-cycle and pricing-logic differences are second nature, because everything here is built on top of them.
What strategy is and isn't
Guards against the most common misuse of this topic, which is treating "we are B2B now" as a strategy. A choice of buyer is a premise; the strategy is what you do about the resulting constraints.
Rumelt's kernel
Diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action. The approval cascade in section 3 is a diagnosis instrument: it tells you which gate is the actual obstacle, which is precisely what Rumelt means by naming the crux rather than listing ambitions.
Risks and assumptions in strategy
Directly applicable to the two numbers that dominate every early B2B case — unobserved renewal rate and unobserved expansion rate. Learning to state these as assumptions with tests attached is the difference between a forecast and a wish.
Playing to Win: where to play, how to win
The natural next frame for the dual-motion question. Koshika and Kovida are both making where-to-play choices; the framework forces the accompanying how-to-win choice, which is where most dual-motion plans are found to be empty.
Product-market fit
Essential complement, because the label tells you nothing about fit. Koyal had consumer fit and no enterprise fit, and the measurement instruments for the two are different: retention curves on one side, renewal and expansion on the other.
Wardley mapping
The best available tool for the claim in section 6 that distribution is the real variable. Mapping components by evolution shows why a capability that required field sales five years ago is self-serve today, and lets you anticipate the motion shift instead of discovering it from a competitor.

B2B vs B2C Strategy: Why the Buyer Changes Everything Downstream

1. A pilot that looks like a lifeline, and a roadmap that cannot serve two masters

On the second Tuesday of March 2025, Tanvi Raghunathan, VP of Product at Tarasha Systems, a fourteen-person startup in Bengaluru's Indiranagar, opened the monthly board deck with a number she had rehearsed twice in the shower. Tanki, the company's consumer app for tracking personal expenses, had 42,000 paying subscribers at ₹99 a month, which produced a tidy ₹41.6 lakh in monthly recurring revenue. The number she had rehearsed was the one under it: month-on-month growth had fallen to 3%, down from 11% a year earlier, and customer acquisition cost had crept up to ₹340 per paying user against a lifetime value she calculated at roughly ₹1,650. The ratio was still healthy on a spreadsheet. It was not healthy on a calendar: at the current growth rate, Tarasha would not clear ₹1 crore in MRR before its eleven months of runway ran out.

The second half of the deck told a different story. Three mid-sized logistics companies — none of them competitors of each other, none of them asked to talk to one another — had independently approached Tarasha in the previous quarter wanting a version of Tanki that their fleet drivers and delivery partners could use to file reimbursable expenses, with a dashboard for the finance team to approve and reconcile them. One of the three, a Pune-based freight operator, had signed a paid pilot: ₹18 lakh a year for roughly 150 driver seats, a number that dwarfed what 150 individual Tanki subscribers would ever have paid Tarasha in a year (₹1.78 lakh). Tanvi's engineering lead had already mocked up an admin console. Her sales-minded co-founder wanted to pull two more engineers off Tanki immediately and chase five more logistics accounts before the fiscal year closed.

What made the room tense was not whether the enterprise opportunity was real — the signed pilot proved that it was — but what pursuing it seriously would actually require of the company, and what the consumer product would have to give up to fund it. Tanvi's job that quarter was to answer a question that looks simple and is not: is this the same business with a bigger invoice, or is it a different business that happens to share some code? Getting that question wrong either way — treating a B2B motion as a bolt-on to a B2C product, or starving a working consumer business to chase enterprise logos that take a year to compound — was the kind of mistake that had quietly killed companies Tanvi had worked at before. This is the decision the rest of this page is built around, because the distinction between selling to businesses and selling to consumers is not a marketing detail. It reorganizes strategy, go-to-market, pricing, and the roadmap itself.

2. The idea: two buyers, two logics

B2B vs B2C strategy is the discipline of designing a company's product, pricing, and go-to-market motion around who the economic buyer is and whether that buyer is the same person as the end user — because that single fact changes how long it takes to close a sale, how the product must earn trust, how price is justified, and what "success" looks like to the person who has to renew the contract or the subscription. In consumer (B2C) businesses, the buyer and the user are almost always the same individual, making an independent, often fast, often emotional decision with their own money. In business (B2B) contexts, the buyer is an organization acting through people who are frequently not the ones who will use the product day to day, spending the organization's money, following a process with multiple approvers, and answerable to colleagues if the choice goes badly.

The distinction is not an academic invention with a single named author and a publication date, the way, say, the Ansoff Matrix or Porter's Five Forces are. It hardened into a practitioner category over the 1990s and 2000s as software separated into two visibly different industries: enterprise software sold by companies like Siebel, SAP and later Salesforce (founded 1999, and instrumental in popularizing the subscription-and-sales-team B2B SaaS model) on one side, and consumer internet businesses — Yahoo, AOL, and later Google and Facebook — built on advertising or micropayments at individual scale on the other. Product managers, sales leaders and investors needed a shorthand for "who are we building this for and how do we get paid," and B2B/B2C became that shorthand. It is best understood not as a rigorous theory but as a lens: a set of questions about the buyer that predicts, with real reliability, what your GTM motion, your pricing model, and your roadmap priorities need to look like.

The sentence Tanvi could say in that board meeting without sounding glib is this: in B2B you are usually selling to someone who will never personally use the product, while in B2C the person who pays and the person who uses it are almost always the same — and that one fact rewires pricing, sales motion, support expectations, and even what counts as an acceptable rate of churn.

"In B2B you are usually selling to someone who will never personally use the product; in B2C the person who pays and the person who uses it are almost always the same — and that one fact rewires everything downstream."

3. The mechanics: what actually changes, step by step

Practitioners rarely walk through this explicitly, which is exactly why it is worth walking through explicitly. There are six things that shift once you know whether your buyer is a business or a consumer, and most teams only discover three of them the hard way.

Step one is mapping the roles. In B2C, one person is user, buyer and decision-maker. In B2B, these usually split into at least three roles: the user (the driver filing an expense claim), the champion or buyer (the finance manager who wants the reconciliation headache to go away), and the approver or gatekeeper (a CFO, or an IT security reviewer, who has to sign off on a new vendor touching payroll-adjacent data). Tanvi's team had built Tanki entirely around the first role. They had never designed for the third.

Step two is the decision unit and cycle length. A consumer decides to subscribe to Tanki in the time it takes to read three reviews and enter a card number — often under ten minutes, frequently on impulse, reversible with one tap. An enterprise logistics company deciding to pay ₹18 lakh a year for driver-expense software runs the decision through a committee: the pilot itself took Tarasha eleven weeks from first call to signature, and included a data-security questionnaire Tanvi's team had never had to answer before.

Step three is choosing the go-to-market motion. Consumer products default to product-led or paid-acquisition motions: app-store listings, referral loops, performance marketing, self-serve sign-up. Business products, especially above a certain contract size, default to sales-led motions: named-account lists, discovery calls, pilots, procurement. Tarasha for Business could not be "download and subscribe" — it needed a salesperson, a pilot period, and a security review before the first invoice was ever raised.

Step four is pricing logic. Consumer pricing tends to be a flat, low, psychologically anchored number the individual pays from a personal budget — ₹99 a month reads as "less than two coffees." Business pricing tends to track a value or usage metric the buyer can defend internally — per seat, per transaction, per driver — because a finance manager has to justify the line item to someone else, not just to their own conscience.

Step five is roadmap prioritization. A consumer roadmap optimizes for features that move engagement and retention across a large, anonymous base — daily-open habits, delightful defaults, low-friction onboarding. A business roadmap optimizes for the handful of features that unblock the next signed deal or prevent the next renewal from being contested — an audit trail, role-based permissions, an export format the client's ERP can ingest.

Step six, the one teams leave implicit until it bites them, is organizational design. A B2C motion can run lean on customer success because support is largely self-serve and failures are individually small. A B2B motion requires named account managers, an implementation function, and support SLAs written into the contract — because losing one enterprise logo is a material revenue event, not a rounding error the way losing one consumer subscriber is.

If Tanvi's team shipped a better onboarding flow and pulled churn down to 4% a month, LTV would rise to ₹99 ÷ 0.04 = ₹2,475, lifting the ratio to 7.3x without changing price or acquisition spend at all — a reminder that in consumer businesses, retention engineering is very often the highest-leverage lever available, more so than acquisition or pricing.

But that arithmetic hides the one number nobody at Tarasha actually had yet: annual logo churn. With only one pilot signed and no renewal date yet reached, any LTV figure Tanvi quoted the board was an assumption dressed as a fact.
