This is why experienced operators discount early B2B LTV:CAC claims heavily, and why Tanvi's most important near-term task, whichever way the board leaned, was to get to a second and third renewal as fast as possible rather than to sign five more logos on the strength of the first.

5. The nuances a learner has to sit with

It is a spectrum, not a pair of boxes

Real companies rarely sit purely on one side. A freelance graphic designer paying for Adobe Creative Cloud with a personal card is technically a consumer transaction for a product that is, in every design decision, built for professional and often small-business use. SMB software sold self-serve — a small retailer subscribing to a billing tool with a debit card, no salesperson involved — behaves like B2C in its GTM motion even though the buyer is nominally a business. Treat B2B and B2C as two ends of a continuum defined by buyer-user overlap and decision-unit size, not as a binary flag on a company profile.

"Who pays" is not the same question as "who decides"

Even within B2B, conflating the champion, the approver and the user into one imagined "customer" is a common and costly error. Tarasha's finance-manager champion loved the product; the IT security reviewer, who Tarasha's team had never spoken to before week nine of the pilot, nearly killed the deal over data-residency questions nobody had prepared an answer for.

B2B2C models split the distinction again

A growing share of Indian fintech and logistics software sells to a business whose end customers are consumers — an insurance API sold to an NBFC that in turn serves retail borrowers, for instance. Here the immediate buyer is a business, but product decisions must also account for a consumer-grade end experience the immediate buyer never directly uses. Neither "B2B" nor "B2C" alone describes the roadmap pressures this creates.

GTM motion and buyer type are correlated, not identical

Sales-led and product-led are choices about distribution; B2B and B2C are facts about the buyer. Most enterprise software is sales-led, and most consumer apps are product-led, but there are self-serve B2B tools (many small-business SaaS products) and heavily sales-assisted B2C purchases (a home solar installation, a luxury watch). Confusing the two means importing the wrong playbook — a sales-led enterprise pricing conversation grafted onto a product genuinely suited to self-serve growth burns cycles for no reason.

The label tells you almost nothing about whether you have product-market fit

Knowing you are "B2B" tells you how to structure a sales team and a pricing sheet. It does not tell you whether logistics companies actually need what Tarasha built, whether the price is right, or whether the feature set solves the problem well enough to renew. Strategy frameworks describe the shape of the game; they do not play it for you.

The distinction weakens at the edges of "prosumer" businesses

Shopify sells to individuals who are legally consumers but are, in every functional sense, running a business; so does a platform selling to independent doctors, lawyers or chartered accountants. These "prosumer" segments need B2B-grade reliability and record-keeping with B2C-grade sign-up speed and pricing psychology — a genuinely harder design brief than either pure case.

"B2B means easy money" is a trap, not an insight

A large contract value is not the same as a profitable one once implementation cost, customization requests, and a longer cash-conversion cycle are counted. Tarasha's ₹18-lakh pilot required two weeks of engineering time to build a custom export format the client's accounting system demanded — a cost invisible in the headline ACV.

The question a thoughtful newcomer should ask before relying on any of this

Before adopting a B2B or B2C playbook wholesale: "Is the change I am making a change of buyer, or does it also require a change of product?" Renaming a consumer app "for teams" and adding an admin login is not the same undertaking as building the audit trails, permissioning, and support commitments an actual enterprise buyer will contractually require.

6. How the picture shifts by product type and by company stage

In a pure consumer product, growth is dominated by acquisition funnels and retention loops measured in days and weeks — Tanki's team watches Day-1 and Day-30 retention the way Tarasha for Business's team watches contract renewal dates, a difference in cadence that alone should tell a PM which motion they are actually running. In a pure B2B product, growth is dominated by named-account pipelines, and the product roadmap answers to procurement and security requirements as often as to end-user delight. In a marketplace, the company runs both motions simultaneously and separately: Swiggy's restaurant-partner side behaves like a B2B sales-and-account-management motion (onboarding, commission negotiation, operational SLAs), while its diner-facing side behaves like classic B2C growth marketing — and treating both sides with one undifferentiated roadmap is a documented way for marketplace product teams to under-serve both.

Company stage changes the picture again. An early-stage B2C company can grow through founder-led hustle, community seeding, and a scrappy referral loop, the way Tanki's first 5,000 users came almost entirely from a WhatsApp-forwarded blog post; at scale, growth becomes an engineering discipline — paid channel mix, lifecycle messaging, statistically rigorous experimentation. An early-stage B2B company can often sell its first five logos through the founders' personal networks with a barely-productised pilot, exactly as Tarasha did; at scale, it needs a repeatable sales playbook, vertical specialization, channel partners, and a support organization that does not depend on the founder personally answering support tickets at midnight. The mistake many teams make is designing the scaled version of the playbook before they have earned the right to — building an enterprise sales team before three logos have renewed, or building a paid-acquisition machine before organic retention curves have flattened.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: treating a B2B pivot as "the same product, a bigger invoice." The symptom is a sales team that closes deals the product cannot actually support — pilots that stall at implementation, champions who go quiet after week six. The underlying misunderstanding is believing that adding an admin panel is equivalent to building for a buying committee. The cheapest diagnostic: ask how many named individuals signed off on your last three deals, and whether your product addresses every one of their concerns, not just the champion's.

Mistake two: running one dashboard, one north-star metric, for two different motions. The symptom is a PM anxiously tracking daily active usage on an enterprise product where low daily usage is actually normal and healthy — a driver only opens the expense app when there is an expense to log. The underlying misunderstanding is importing a consumer engagement metric wholesale into a context where the correct metric is outcome-based (claims processed correctly, hours saved for the finance team) rather than frequency-based. The cheapest diagnostic: ask whether the metric you are optimizing is one the paying buyer has ever mentioned caring about.

Mistake three: pricing the wrong model onto the wrong buyer. The symptom, on the B2B side, is money quietly left on the table — a flat consumer-style price that does not scale with the value a large account actually receives, so a 500-seat client pays the same as a 20-seat one. On the B2C side, the symptom is a killed conversion funnel — an annual-contract, sales-assisted pricing page grafted onto a product individual users expected to try in minutes. The underlying misunderstanding, in both directions, is copying a pricing structure because it is fashionable in software rather than because it matches how this particular buyer justifies the spend. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the buyer, out loud, how they would explain this price to whoever they report to — an answer that takes more than one sentence is a warning sign.

Mistake four: quoting an early B2B LTV:CAC ratio as if it were proven. The symptom is a board deck, like the one Tanvi almost presented, showing a 20x return on the strength of one unrenewed pilot. The underlying misunderstanding is forgetting that LTV for a B2B product is a forecast built almost entirely on an assumed churn rate nobody has actually observed yet. The cheapest diagnostic: recompute the same ratio at two or three plausible churn assumptions, as in Table 2, before anyone repeats the optimistic number out loud.

8. What good looks like

A useful real-world portrait is Freshworks (known for its first years as Freshdesk), founded in Chennai in 2010. The company built a customer-support product and, crucially, refused to force every customer through a single motion. Small support teams could sign up, get value within minutes, and pay by credit card with no salesperson involved — a genuinely self-serve, product-led B2B motion, priced per agent seat in a way a small business owner could justify without asking anyone's permission. As accounts grew larger and the buyer shifted toward IT and procurement teams at bigger enterprises, the same company layered on a sales-led motion — named account managers, security documentation, negotiated multi-year contracts — for exactly the segment where that additional cost was worth paying. What made this "good" was not cleverness in either motion alone; it was the discipline of running two distinct GTM engines against two honestly different buyer profiles inside one company, rather than forcing every prospect through one undifferentiated funnel, or pretending the self-serve motion could handle every deal size on its own. The product itself stayed largely unified; the go-to-market machinery, pricing conversation, and support commitment did not.

9. What Tanvi decided, and what to sit with next

Tanvi did not choose between Tanki and Tarasha for Business, and she did not try to run them off one backlog either. She proposed, and the board approved, a segmented dual-motion plan for the next two quarters: three of Tarasha's fourteen engineers, plus one of the two founders' selling time, would go toward Tarasha for Business, with an explicit gate — no further headcount would move to the enterprise track until at least two of the pilot logos renewed past their first annual contract, giving the company real churn data instead of an assumption. The remaining engineering majority stayed on Tanki, with the single quarterly objective of moving monthly churn from 6% toward 4%, since that lever alone was worth more to the consumer business's economics than any acquisition spend increase. Separate pricing pages, separate onboarding flows, and — most importantly — separate success metrics were assigned to each motion, so that no single dashboard would quietly force one buyer's logic onto the other's product.

The reasoning underneath the decision was simple to state and hard to have arrived at without walking through the mechanics above: the enterprise opportunity was real, but its attractiveness on paper depended entirely on a renewal number Tarasha did not yet have, while the consumer business, though slower-growing, was a known, measurable quantity that could fund the company's runway while the enterprise bet proved itself. What Tanvi would want to learn next is how to design pricing that survives contact with each buyer type's justification process — value-based pricing for the enterprise seats, and psychologically calibrated pricing for the consumer subscription — since getting the price right is the natural next lever once the buyer and the motion have been correctly identified.

Two questions worth sitting with, whether the product in front of you is Tarasha's or your own:

  • If you shipped one feature this quarter, whose meeting would it need to survive before it ever reached a paying user — and is that person someone your roadmap currently accounts for at all?
  • What share of this quarter's roadmap is aimed at a buyer nobody on the product team has ever actually spoken to?

Viraam Charge Networks: The Plug and the Contract

Three revenue lines, one balance sheet, eight months of cash. Before the board meets, Viraam's chief product officer must say which business the company is in — and the question may have no answer as posed.

Strategy & Business · Product Strategy · Case 40

1. Ninety-six Hours Before the Board

At twenty past eleven on the night of Thursday, 20 August 2026, the monsoon over Domlur was loud enough that Nikhil Sarangi could hear it through the sealed windows of Viraam Charge Networks' fourth-floor office in Bengaluru. On his laptop sat two versions of slide nine of the board pre-read, saved eleven minutes apart: "FY27 Plan — Consumer-Led" and "FY27 Plan — Fleet & Platform." The board met on Monday, 24 August. Vitaan Growth Partners had offered ₹240 crore to extend the Series B, and the fund's Singapore partner had written a sentence Nikhil had read thirty times: we are underwriting one company, and we cannot yet tell which one it is.

Viraam had closed FY26 with ₹138 crore of revenue across three lines that behaved like three separate businesses. It ran 1,412 charging points in nineteen Indian cities, licensed its charge-point management software, Grid OS, to operators in four countries, and held a Dubai contract worth more than any Indian customer it had signed. On the treasury sheet in a second window: ₹61 crore against a burn of ₹7.4 crore a month.

Nikhil, thirty-nine, had joined as chief product officer in 2023 from a payments company, hired to make the app the reason a driver chose one charger. Since then he had written roadmaps for a company that was, depending on the meeting, a consumer brand, an industrial energy supplier, or a software vendor. He had built both versions of slide nine because he could defend either and believed neither. What he had not found, anywhere in his data room, was something that settled the argument rather than restating it.

2. How Viraam Came to Own 1,412 Plugs

Sharmila Bhatt had spent eleven years financing transmission and solar projects before she and Ravi Kulkarni, a power-electronics engineer in Pune, incorporated Viraam in March 2019. The founding thesis was consumer-shaped: India would have millions of electric vehicles before it had any coherent way to charge them, and the scarce asset would be trust — that the plug would work and the price would not surprise. For two years Viraam owned no hardware: its app aggregated third-party chargers, took UPI payments through an NPCI-rails partner, and sold nothing but reliability.

That worked until it did not. Aggregation gave Viraam no control over uptime, and uptime was the promise. In 2021 it raised its Series A and began installing its own 60 kW DC points. In 2023 came the decision that defines its present. Urban parking with a usable electrical connection was then the genuinely scarce commodity; Tata Power, Jio-bp pulse, Statiq and ChargeZone were bidding for the same mall basements. Sharmila signed a seven-year exclusive site-hosting agreement with Vaastu Realty Partners covering 58 retail properties in eight cities: ₹2.4 crore per quarter guaranteed regardless of throughput, against first refusal on every new Vaastu development until 2030.

The agreement contained a clause nobody argued about. Vaastu's tenants were retailers; footfall was the point. Every Viraam bay on a Vaastu property had to stay open to the public during mall hours and could not be reserved, gated or assigned to one commercial operator. In 2023 this read as boilerplate. In 2026 it meant 40 per cent of installed capacity, on the most expensive real estate Viraam paid for, could not become the fleet depots its fastest-growing customers wanted — and that ₹38.4 crore of guarantee was payable over four years in every scenario Nikhil could model.

3. The Industry Around It

By 2026 the Indian charging market had split into segments sharing equipment and almost nothing else. Private four-wheeler owners, the customers Viraam was founded to serve, took most of their kilowatt-hours at home or at the office; public fast charging was for anxiety, highways and the festival drive to Mysuru. Tata Power and Jio-bp pulse had deep balance sheets and captive real estate; Ather Grid had made its network a feature of its scooters rather than a business. The Ministry of Power's guidelines had de-licensed public charging and pushed states toward separate EV tariffs, but demand charges still fell on operators, and eighteen per cent GST on charging sat awkwardly against five per cent on the vehicles.

The segment actually growing was commercial. Delivery fleets running for Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto and Amazon India, e-auto and e-taxi operators, and the last-mile arms of larger groups had electrified fast because their arithmetic was fuel arithmetic. They charged in daylight, in bulk, on schedules, and negotiated like the industrial buyers they were: dedicated bays, guaranteed availability, a ₹/kWh number fixed for twenty-four months — not an app with a loyalty tier.

Viraam's third exposure was neither. Grid OS, written to run Viraam's own hardware, had been licensed since 2024 to two networks in the United States, one in Germany and one in the Gulf: standards-compliant, unglamorous, the only line with software margins. It had also brought Viraam its largest customer, Vaseela Mobility LLC, a Dubai e-taxi operator running 900 electric sedans, which signed in January 2026 for Grid OS plus operations support at ₹34 crore over three years. Vaseela's ambitions ran to Sharjah and Abu Dhabi, and its chief operating officer had begun using the word "partner" in a way that implied roadmap influence.

4. What Happened, and What Has Turned Out to Be Wrong

The clean version, as told in the FY26 investor update, ran: the consumer network builds brand and density; fleet contracts fill the idle hours; software monetises the intellectual property twice. Each claim had since been tested, and each came back damaged differently.

The consumer claim was tested by utilisation. Across the Vaastu portfolio, FY26 utilisation averaged 11.4 per cent — respectable for India, nowhere near the level at which a ₹14.5 lakh point pays for itself in a financing cycle. Mall dwell time, the 2023 thesis, turned out to be forty minutes of shopping against ninety of charging, and drivers left at sixty per cent. Nikhil's team responded as consumer teams do — reservations, a ₹499 subscription tier, promotions at Onam and Ganesh Chaturthi — and moved utilisation a point and a half.

The fleet claim was tested by contract. In February 2025 Viraam signed Vihaan Fleet Mobility, a Bengaluru operator with 2,400 e-autos and delivery two-wheelers, on a take-or-pay of 1.9 crore kWh a year at ₹14.50/kWh — twenty-two per cent below realised retail. The assumption was complementarity: fleets in the trough, retail in the evening peak, one asset earning twice. Exhibit 3 was produced to prove it and, read quickly, does. Read slowly, it shows Vihaan's heaviest blocks are midday and late night, that midday is where retail had been climbing, and that queueing at eleven shared sites coincided with the sharpest fall in app-store rating Viraam had recorded.

The software claim was tested by attention. Grid OS grew from ₹2 crore in FY24 to ₹19 crore in FY26 at seventy-one per cent margin, with fourteen engineers and no marketing. When Vaseela signed, two of the four engineers on the app rebuild moved to the Dubai integration within a fortnight; the rebuild, promised for June, had slipped twice. Katrin Obermeyer, who led design from Berlin, had begun calling the app "the thing we keep apologising to."

A fourth thing, unplanned, had corrupted the evidence. In March 2026 the analytics SDK was migrated, and Viraam's consumer metrics had since counted Vihaan drivers' sessions — they used the same app, a separate one having been deferred — inside the consumer funnel. Every engagement number after March described a population Nikhil could not describe.

8. Three Doors, as Nikhil Has Drawn Them

Door one: be a consumer network

Fund the app rebuild, hold the Vaastu portfolio, price for the private driver, let the Vihaan take-or-pay run to term. Accepts plan A's ₹144 crore and bets Indian charging follows the European path with a five-year lag. Requires believing Exhibit 4 over Exhibit 2.

Door two: be a fleet energy supplier

Convert every site the Vaastu clause permits into depot operations, chase Vihaan's expansion and two logistics fleets, win on availability and reconciliation. Delivers plan B's revenue at six per cent margin on the largest line, and concentrates the company in customers who negotiate annually and can build depots themselves.

Door three: be a platform company

Treat the Indian network as a reference installation, licence Grid OS globally, let Vaseela's parent take a stake. Highest margin, smallest base, and the door Sharmila has never mentioned to the board.

Nikhil had drawn the doors on a whiteboard in July and been uneasy with them since. Each describes a customer; none describes the asset. Viraam owns 1,412 points on one balance sheet, under one set of DISCOM contracts, in a country where the consumer and the fleet driver plug into the same socket. Anjali had noted in his margin that a business can sell the same kilowatt-hour to two customers at two prices only while it can keep them apart in time and space — and that the 2023 contract had already decided how much of that separation Viraam could buy. Serena had asked whether "consumer" and "fleet" were customers at all, or two demand curves on one utility, in which case the question was not who to serve but what price discipline the network could hold.

9. The Deadline and What Cannot Be Moved

The board sits on Monday, 24 August. The Vitaan term sheet expires on 30 September, its diligence question — which company is this — written into the conditions precedent. Vaseela wants an answer by 15 October. Cash of ₹61 crore against ₹7.4 crore a month leaves eight months, and the revolving facility is secured against assets valued on Exhibit 2's first column.

The Vaastu agreement runs to 2030, and its public-access clause survives any change of strategy. The Vihaan contract carries a take-or-pay of 1.9 crore kWh a year and a three-kilometre exclusivity radius around each shared site, foreclosing several depots Fatima had shortlisted. Thirty-four people work on the consumer product, nineteen in Bengaluru on three-month notice; a hiring freeze has run since May. The DPDP Act consent re-architecture, on which app and fleet portal both depend, faces external review in November and is resourced for one of them.
